rawInput.complaint: A 90-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a gradually enlarging left-sided nasal mass. He had no prior sinus disease or surgery. On examination, a voluminous mass was prolapsing through the left nostril, causing complete obstruction of the left nasal cavity and deflecting the nasal septum to the right; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy or facial deformity. Nasal endoscopy via the right naris revealed a smooth, grayish mass filling the left choana and extending into the nasopharyngeal space, displacing the septum. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a homogeneous mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity and extending to the nasopharynx, displacing the medial wall of the left maxillary sinus; erosion of the nasal septum and the left lamina papyracea was noted, along with complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief complaint is a 4-month history of a gradually enlarging unilateral left nasal mass in a 90-year-old man, with the patient’s main concern being progressive nasal obstruction from a mass prolapsing through the left nostril. The unilateral nature, progressive enlargement, and extension into the choana/nasopharynx immediately raise concern for a sinonasal neoplasm rather than simple inflammatory disease.

Salient positive findings are: advanced age (90 years), a large smooth grayish mass arising in the left nasal cavity, complete obstruction of the left nasal cavity, septal deviation to the right from mass effect, extension posteriorly into the left choana and nasopharyngeal space, and CT showing a homogeneous lesion completely occupying the left nasal cavity with extension to the nasopharynx. Importantly, CT also shows erosion of the nasal septum and left lamina papyracea and displacement of the medial wall of the left maxillary sinus, with complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus. These bony changes suggest a locally expansile/destructive process. The absence of prior sinus surgery is relevant because it argues strongly against an antrochoanal polyp arising as a postoperative maxillary sinus lesion or postoperative maxillary mucocele.

Pertinent negatives include no prior sinus disease or surgery, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and no facial deformity. Lack of lymphadenopathy does not exclude malignancy but makes advanced nodal metastatic disease less evident. No history is given of epistaxis, pain, cranial neuropathy, or facial swelling, which somewhat lowers suspicion for an aggressive invasive carcinoma, though absence of these symptoms does not rule it out.

The first major differential is an antrochoanal polyp because the mass is smooth, grayish, unilateral, fills the choana, extends into the nasopharynx, and there is complete opacification of the ipsilateral maxillary sinus. Those are classic features of a choanal polyp arising from the maxillary sinus. However, antrochoanal polyps are more typical in children and young adults, and they usually cause remodeling rather than frank erosion of structures such as the nasal septum and lamina papyracea. In a 90-year-old with septal and orbital wall erosion, a simple inflammatory polyp becomes less convincing.

A second strong consideration is inverted papilloma. This typically presents as a unilateral nasal mass in older adults, often causes nasal obstruction, can extend into the maxillary sinus and choana, and is known for local aggressiveness with bone remodeling/erosion. The unilateral origin, age group, expansile behavior, and associated maxillary sinus opacification fit well. Although CT classically may show a unilateral soft-tissue mass with sinus involvement and bony remodeling, the description here of a smooth gray mass and homogeneous lesion is compatible. Inverted papilloma is therefore a very plausible diagnosis.

Sinonasal malignancy such as squamous cell carcinoma must also be considered because unilateral nasal mass with bone erosion in an elderly patient is concerning. Erosion of the lamina papyracea and septum could reflect malignant invasion. However, the lesion is described as smooth and homogeneous rather than irregular or necrotic, and there is no cervical lymphadenopathy, facial deformity, or other aggressive symptoms provided. Malignancy remains possible but is somewhat less favored than a benign but locally aggressive epithelial tumor.

Other possibilities are less likely. An ordinary inflammatory nasal polyp is less likely because it is usually bilateral and associated with chronic rhinosinusitis; here there is no prior sinus disease and there is destructive change. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is implausible given the patient’s age and lack of typical demographic profile. Mucocele is less likely because the lesion is intranasal/choanal and prolapsing through the nostril rather than a sinus-expansile cystic lesion.

Narrowing to the single most likely diagnosis: the combination of an elderly patient, unilateral nasal cavity mass, extension into the choana/nasopharynx, ipsilateral maxillary sinus involvement, and local bony erosion/remodeling most strongly supports inverted papilloma over a simple antrochoanal polyp. While sinonasal carcinoma remains an important alternative because of the bone erosion, the gross description and imaging pattern are more in keeping with inverted papilloma, a benign but locally aggressive sinonasal tumor.

differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Older adult with unilateral left nasal mass causing obstruction, extension into choana/nasopharynx, ipsilateral maxillary sinus opacification, and local bony erosion/remodeling of the septum and lamina papyracea.

Smooth gray unilateral mass filling the choana and extending into the nasopharynx with complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus fits a choanal polyp pattern, but age 90 and bony erosion make this less likely.

Elderly patient with unilateral nasal mass and bone erosion of the septum and lamina papyracea raises concern for malignancy, though the lesion is described as smooth and homogeneous without lymphadenopathy or facial deformity.

Can appear smooth and grayish, but usually occurs with chronic rhinosinusitis and often bilaterally; destructive bony changes and unilateral large expansile behavior argue against a simple inflammatory polyp.
